newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda says it will bar Tutsi men fleeing Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda says it will bar Tutsi men fleeing Zaire.

text.p: Rwanda's president vowed on Thursday to bar ethnic Tutsi men ordered to leave Zaire next week or face all-out war as rebels.
President Pasteur Bizimungu told a rally in the Rwandan border town of Cyangugu facing eastern Zaire: "We will only be taking women and children. The men will have to stay where they are."
"We will be persuading the (Banyamulenge) men who are in Rwanda already to return to Zaire. Zaire needs to accept that the Banyamulenge are also Zaireans," the Hutu president added.
Some 500 Tutsi Banyamulenge had fled into Rwanda in recent weeks because of an upsurge in fighting between the Zairean army, Banyamulenge armed groups and other Zairean armed groups.

Denouncing a virtual state of war in eastern Zaire, South Kivu deputy governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabanji on Tuesday gave the estimated 200,000 Banyamulenge Tutsis one week to leave or be treated as rebels and face all-out war with Zairean soldiers.

Conflict between the army and Banyamulenge, who have been denied Zairean citizenship, has been growing for months. The Banyamulenge are ethnic Tutsis who arrived in eastern Zaire up to 200 years ago from what are now Rwanda and Burundi.

Zairean authorities have whipped up public opinion against the Banyamulenge and diplomats fear conflict could spread as the mainly Tutsi armies in Rwanda and Burundi may decide to support their kinfolk.
Bizmungu said Cyangugu, adjacent to the Zairean town of Bukavu, was caught in its biggest security crisis since Rwanda's genocide of up to one million people in 1994 and French military intervention.

"The point of my visit here is to assure protection of Rwandan territory, and to demonstrate that an attack on Cyangugu would mean an attack on all Rwanda. We are going to stay in place to give the Zaireans a lesson," the president said.

"Rwanda and Rwandans are going to defend themselves after each attack," said Bizimungu, accompanied on his one-day visit to Cyangugu by the army chief of staff, his prime minister and other officials.
Cyangugu Prefect Faustin Monyakibira denounced killings of Banyamulenge in south Kivu as "genocide" and said firing from Zaire last week cut down the amount of traffic on Lake Kivu and roads.
Rwandan and Zairean troops exchanged fire between Bukavu and Cyangugu late last month after human rights groups accused the Zairean army of carrying out atrocities against Banyamulenge.
Zairean authorities want to concentrate the Banyamulenge in government-controlled camps to make them easier to monitor.

Aid agencies say they are prepared for an influx of Banyamulenge into Rwanda from eastern Zaire, which is also home to 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus who fled their homeland during the genocide by Hutu forces and mobs and three months of civil war.
On Tuesday Bukavu was shaken by more than an hour of gunfire by Zairean troops after the bodies of an army colonel and six soldiers killed in fighting with Banyamulenge arrived in town.
Zaire's army is notoriously indisciplined. Soldiers say their pay is a pittance and they turn to crime to survive.
